title: Jack × Caryn
summary: Jack pitched Caryn, a substitute teacher finishing a degree, with the standard outcome script (job in 3-6 weeks, $60-80K remote junior, six-figure senior in 6-9 months, two paid internships, internship income covers the loan and the job covers tuition) and then spent the last twenty minutes pushing past her request to talk to her husband and start on the 23rd, including a Lamborghini analogy to her cost concern and a likely wrong statement that there is no credit pull for 45 days. He did get several things right (guarantee conditions minus documentation, total tuition and monthly figure before the application, the earn-while-you-learn hedge, telling her she does not have to say yes), but the prohibited income and loan-payoff claims plus the override of her think-about-it request make this serious.
coverage: Full transcript reviewed, 365 speaker segments from 0:00 to 1:08:17. The recording ends while Caryn is still trying to share her screen for the Climb Credit application, so the application walkthrough, any PII handling, agreement review and signing, and whether she enrolled could not be reviewed; a Monday follow-up and an onboarding call were discussed. Speaker labels are scrambled in several places (some of Jack's questions appear under Caryn's name, e.g. 05:04, 15:12, 26:23, 38:14, 50:53), so attribution was judged from content; two connection drops (35:36 and 1:05-1:07) lose a few seconds. The setter is referred to as Harry; Caryn's last name is not said.

findings.quote: After finishing, a complete beginner usually lands their first role within three to six weeks. And that first role is always a junior position.
findings.note: A 3-6 week time-to-job is presented as the usual outcome; this is a P14 claim to remove immediately and no employment timeframe is contractually committed.

findings.quote: Juniors usually start around like 60 to 80K a year and the roles are completely remote.
findings.note: A specific starting-salary band and fully remote work are presented as the typical graduate outcome with no substantiation or qualification.

findings.quote: from junior, our students are going to transition to a senior position within about six to nine months. And those seniors are going to be the guys in that six figure range.
findings.note: Rapid progression to a six-figure senior role within 6-9 months is stated as what will happen, implying exceptional outcomes are typical.

findings.quote: we're going to teach you from week two how to build and sell projects for businesses. They're from $500 to $1,500 each. Now this does three things.
findings.note: Earn-while-you-learn income of $500-$1,500 per project from week two is presented as expected, and the same passage says 'our students get hired over people with four-year degrees' as a general fact.

findings.quote: in this bootcamp, you get placed in two paid internships with AI tech companies that we partner with. Obviously, you're going to get paid.
findings.note: Every student is told they will receive two paid internships with no mention of selection, eligibility, capacity or timing, which is the 'everyone gets the internship' claim.

findings.quote: all 17 of our mentors. They're in this channel. You'll get a response within 15 minutes, 24-7.
findings.note: A guaranteed 15-minute response around the clock is a specific support promise that must match what is actually delivered.

findings.quote: To qualify, all you've got to do is complete the bootcamp. You've got to apply to 30 positions a week, but we automate all that. We'll show you how to do that. It takes like one sitting.
findings.note: The documented-job-search requirement is never mentioned, the 30-per-week condition is minimized as automated and quick, and how a refund interacts with the Climb loan, interest and fees is not explained.

findings.quote: they get a full refund of the tuition plus $1,000 on top.
findings.note: The extra $1,000 should be verified against the written Job Guarantee; if it is not documented it is a promised undocumented benefit.

findings.quote: So you put no money down for the first month and a half. After that, the monthly payments, they're around 250 bucks, maybe 20 bucks more, maybe 20 bucks less.
findings.note: The monthly figure is quoted without the loan term, interest rate, total repayment amount or a statement that the numbers depend on lender approval and may change.

findings.quote: the full bootcamp, including the job guarantee is just 10k. Now, obviously, nobody pays for that upfront. So we can relax.
findings.note: Tuition and financing are explained in full but the 14-day cancellation window and the written refund and cancellation policy are never mentioned anywhere in the recording.

findings.quote: Once we land the job, you either keep making those small monthly payments or do what most students do. What is use a few paychecks to pay it off sooner.
findings.note: 'Pay the loan off with your first few paychecks' is a P14 claim to remove immediately, and 'once we land the job' implies FES places the student.

findings.quote: the money you earn from the internship and the earn while you learn will cover the monthlies until you land the job. Job covers tuition.
findings.note: Program income covering the loan payments and the job covering tuition is stated as fact, i.e. the loan pays for itself, and it contradicts the 'not typical' hedge given a minute earlier.

findings.quote: So you could, in theory, have a job by then.
findings.note: Even with the 'in theory' hedge, this ties employment to a specific date (her May 4 graduation), implying a job timeframe.

findings.quote: This can get you to where you want to go. And I know it can. I know you'll be successful here.
findings.note: Personal assurance of success stated as certainty to a prospect who had just described stress over mortgage and bills.

findings.quote: given that it's been a few years, we've been allowing this self-doubt to get in the way. What do you think that self-doubt in the past has cost us?
findings.note: After the prospect disclosed an abusive marriage, a mother with Alzheimer's and money stress, the closer builds urgency on self-doubt and later on what she would tell her daughter (24:33), which exploits personal distress to drive a decision.

findings.quote: I'm sure like Jason sounds like a legend, but this is being speaking candidly, speaking candidly, Caryn, at the end of the day, whose career is it we're talking about here?
findings.note: The prospect clearly asked to talk to her husband and proposed a Monday follow-up; the closer repeatedly reframes that as a question of who controls her life (50:20-51:25) rather than accepting the request to think it over.

findings.quote: do you think that's a problem? Or do you think that's a symptom of the problem? Because if you were working a tech job right now, you wouldn't necessarily have a crazy planner right now, would you?
findings.note: Her stated reason for not deciding today (a fully booked schedule) is reframed as a personal failing to push a same-call commitment.

findings.quote: why don't we just get you started? I guess now? And we can officially put the start date on the 23rd. Like you're not going to be having to make a payment for another four weeks after that anyway.
findings.note: After she asked to start on the 23rd and speak to her husband first, the closer pushes signing the loan today using the payment deferral as the reason to commit now.

findings.quote: Cause if I offered you a Lamborghini for 10,000, you'd be like, well, that's very cheap. But if I offered you a dinner for 10,000, you'd be like, wow, that's very expensive.
findings.note: Her 'that's a lot of money right now' objection is answered with an analogy instead of being addressed, dismissing a financial-hardship concern.

findings.quote: They're called Climb Credit. They're like a multi-million dollar organization. We've got a pretty big deal with them. It's like for student loans. And basically, you just run through that. It's what? 99% of the people.
findings.note: '99% of the people' is an unsubstantiated statistic and 'a pretty big deal with them' suggests a special arrangement with the lender.

findings.quote: Again, your credit won't actually get, like, there won't be a pull for 45 days. And would you rather have 650 credit or like 640 credit and this skill set at your disposal?
findings.note: A lender application normally involves a credit check at application time, so telling her there is no pull for 45 days likely misstates loan terms, and her credit concern is brushed aside.

findings.quote: What's the point of having good credit if you're not utilizing it for the things that you really want, you know?
findings.note: Encourages taking on debt as a matter of principle in response to a nervous prospect, which pressures rather than informs.

findings.quote: this bootcamp is three months at like one to two hours a day. So like five to 10 hours a week. And obviously it's self-paced, which means you're the boss.
findings.note: A self-paced program is framed as a fixed three-month duration, and later the guarantee example assumes finishing in a month, even though she said she can only commit about two hours a day.

compliant.note: Stated bootcamp completion, 30 applications per week and the 12-month window as conditions, and said it is not a magic pill and the student has to do the work.
Said there is no crystal ball of certainty and the future cannot be predicted before asking for commitment.
Gave the $10k total tuition, the 45-day no-payment period and an approximate $250 monthly payment before any lender application.
Explicitly said he did not want to give the idea that earn-while-you-learn covers full tuition and that it is not typical.
Described support as a channel of 17 mentors with live coaching calls, not a single dedicated mentor.
Said he was not suggesting dropping anything and that only a couple of hours a week would be fair given her schedule.
Told the prospect she does not have to say yes to anything or do anything right now before the application.
No SSN, DOB, card number or address was read aloud in the portion recorded; the recording ended before the application was opened.

title: Jack × Zack Bowden
summary: Jack enrolled Zack Bowden (wife Anna present) on a $10K loan at 23% APR after presenting a 3-6 week time-to-job, $60-80k remote starting salary and 'job covers tuition' as the normal outcome, then coached the lender income field ('put in 60K regardless'), told him the disclosure did not need reading, and walked him click-by-click through accepting the loan agreement. The 14-day cancellation window was never mentioned and the Job Guarantee omitted the documented-search requirement, though tuition, monthly estimate, finance charge and 'not a magic pill' caveats were stated.
coverage: Full 51:52 transcript (302 segments) read end to end; single conversation with prospect Zack Bowden and his wife Anna. Fathom labels both Zack and Anna as 'Zoom user', and at least one Jack segment (36:49 tuition explanation) is mislabelled 'Zoom user'; attribution was inferred from content. Transcript starts mid-greeting so any recording-consent statement before 00:00 is not visible. Several long gaps (40:00-42:00, 45:00-47:00, 48:30-50:00) are screen-share silence while the application was completed; anything typed on screen is not in the transcript.

findings.quote: After finishing, a complete beginner usually lands their first role within about three to six weeks. That first role is a junior position. Juniors are usually starting around 60 to 80k a year mark, and the roles are completely remote
findings.note: States a 3-6 week time-to-job, a $60-80k starting salary and fully remote roles as the normal outcome, which are the exact claims the FTC audit lists for immediate removal.

findings.quote: From junior, our students typically get promoted to a senior position within, like, six to nine months. Seniors are in that six-figure range.
findings.note: Implies rapid junior-to-senior progression and six-figure pay as typical with no substantiation, hedged only by 'typically'.

findings.quote: you either keep making those small monthly payments up to you or do what most students do is use a few paychecks to pay it off sooner. Until you land the job, job covers tuition.
findings.note: Tells the prospect the job will cover the tuition and that most students pay the loan off with a few paychecks, which is the prohibited 'pay the loan off with your first few paychecks' framing.

findings.quote: And then for yearly income, I'm not sure what you earn, Jack, but put in 60K regardless. We get the best terms for that.
findings.note: Coaches the applicant on what income figure to enter in the lender application ('put in 60K regardless'), and also directs the loan amount and 60-month term selection.

findings.quote: Now, this is an example disclosure. So. You don't really need to worry about it, basically. Now, you can read it if you want, but it's going to have no relevance to the loan that we're about to generate.
findings.note: Tells the applicant the lender disclosure does not need to be read, then at 43:19 walks him through 'click I agree and acknowledge' and 'I consent' without pausing.

findings.quote: 284, a 23% interest rate, but the beauty of this is that you actually get to dodge the interest once you pay this thing off in eight months. So that's 23%, that's only on the monthly.
findings.note: Misrepresents the loan terms: interest accrues from day one on a 23% APR loan and is not 'dodged' by early payoff, and 'only on the monthly' is not a meaningful description of APR.

findings.quote: But when you pay this whole thing off, it'll be the $10K minus the monthly payments you've already made.
findings.note: Inaccurate payoff math: monthly payments include interest, so the payoff balance is not principal minus payments made; this understates the cost of the loan.

findings.quote: Click yet sign in, go to application, you can X this for now, and then go accept loan agreement, and then continue to sign. Pick student borrower when you're good to go.
findings.note: Walks the applicant click-by-click through accepting and signing the loan agreement while talking over him about onboarding, with no invitation to read the agreement first.

findings.quote: this finance charge, you see that's 7k, now that's only if you end up paying this for the full 60 month term. Now if you end up paying this for 60 months, Zack, I'm going to personally fly to Florida
findings.note: Points at the $7k finance charge but immediately dismisses it as 'unprecedented', implying the loan will certainly be paid off early from job income.

findings.quote: you've got to apply to 30 developer positions a week. Now, what that means, it's not you manually doing it. We have agent tools in place where you can do all that in a sitting
findings.note: Job Guarantee explained without the documented-job-search requirement or how a refund interacts with the loan balance, and the 30-applications rule is trivialised as something tools do 'in a sitting'.

findings.quote: they're entitled to a full refund of the tuition, plus $1,000 on top. That job, if you don't land a role, is minimum $60,000 a year position.
findings.note: Promises a $1,000 bonus on top of the refund and frames the guarantee around a minimum $60k role; both need to match the written Job Guarantee agreement exactly.

findings.quote: So we're going to place you in two separate paid internships with AI tech companies that we partner with. Yes, you're going to get paid.
findings.note: Presents two paid internships with partner companies as certain for every student, with no mention of selection, eligibility or capacity; repeated at 46:58 ('we're going to be paying you for the internship').

findings.quote: from week two, we're going to show you how to build and sell projects for businesses. Anywhere from 500 bucks. To 1500 bucks each. Number two, you're earning extra income from week two.
findings.note: Earn-while-you-learn income of $500-1,500 per project from week two is presented as expected rather than possible.

findings.quote: Nothing for 45 days. And by then, I think it's like 85% of students. 85% of students have made enough to cover the first month by then.
findings.note: Quotes an unsubstantiated '85% of students' earnings statistic to reassure the prospect about affordability of the first payment.

findings.quote: As long as you can give me five to 10 hours a week, that's the key here. I know that we can help you reach your goals. I know that you'll be successful here, Jax.
findings.note: Tells the prospect he will be successful if he puts in 5-10 hours a week, which implies a guaranteed outcome despite the earlier 'no crystal ball' caveat.

findings.quote: you could define what's been going on in your situation as comfort, but another way of defining it would potentially be settling.
findings.note: After the prospect disclosed hardship paying rent and groceries (09:20), the closer frames his caution as 'settling' and later elicits 'time to grow a set of balls', pressure that exploits financial distress and fear of change.

findings.quote: every single time that someone's unsuccessful, it's not down to the business model. It always comes down to the person. It always comes down to their commitment levels.
findings.note: Attributes every unsuccessful outcome to the student, pre-empting any future complaint and overstating certainty of the program's results.

findings.quote: Link one is like our job guarantee agreement, which is basically just like, you know, we signed that bad boy.
findings.note: At no point in the call is the 14-day cancellation window or refund policy mentioned, and the guarantee agreement is signed in about 15 seconds with no prompt to read it.

findings.quote: What's a ballpark on your credit score, by the way? [redacted] That's good. That's good. you'll get approved.
findings.note: Assures the applicant he will be approved before any lender decision; the prospect's credit score range was also stated aloud on the recording.

findings.quote: Yes, I'll go to your emails. Hope I don't see any illicit material here now. Okay, we're good. Click yet sign in, go to application
findings.note: The prospect's email inbox and lender portal, including income and loan details, were screen-shared on a recorded call; no SSN or DOB was read aloud in the transcript.

findings.quote: you'll have to go back with these guys around the clock. They're across a few different time zones. You can schedule an unlimited number of one-to-ones with these senior software engineers.
findings.note: 'Around the clock' and 'unlimited' one-to-ones may overstate support hours and access; describe exactly as delivered.

findings.quote: this whole program, it takes three months. Like you're your own boss. It's self-paced.
findings.note: Describes a self-paced program as a fixed three-month duration (and later 'if you finish the bootcamp in a month'), which is inconsistent and may understate real completion time.

findings.quote: then after that, then it's around 250 a month, maybe 20 bucks more, maybe 20 bucks less.
findings.note: The pre-application monthly estimate of $230-270 was exceeded by the actual $284 payment, and the gap was not acknowledged when the real terms appeared.

findings.quote: I think 13% of resumes are actually viewed by human eyes. Which means that 87% of them, they get blocked by AI.
findings.note: Unsubstantiated AI/labour-market statistic presented as fact.

compliant.note: Stated the full bootcamp including the Job Guarantee is $10K before starting the application.
Gave an estimated monthly payment (~$250, plus or minus $20) and the 45-day no-payment start before opening the lender application.
Explicitly said 'I don't want to give you the idea that the earn while you learn will cover the full tuition... usually it doesn't.'
Said 'this isn't a magic pill... You still have to do the work' and 'there's no crystal ball of certainty here'.
Acknowledged 'it's not like everybody's successful'.
Stated bootcamp completion, 30 applications per week, and the 12-month / 6-month-of-search window when describing the guarantee.
Described support as a team of 14 senior engineers across time zones, not a single 24/7 mentor.

compliant.area: Finance charge and APR read aloud
compliant.note: Pointed at the $7k finance charge and read the 23% rate and $284 monthly payment aloud on screen.
Told the applicant he could opt out of weekly lender texts.

title: Jack × Ayshia
summary: Jack gave Ayshia (a 23-year-old earning about $1,500 a month) the full outcome pitch as expected results: a junior role in 3-6 weeks at ~$70K remote, senior and six figures in 6-9 months, two guaranteed paid internships, and a 60-month loan that 'nobody' pays for longer than 7-8 months because the job covers the tuition. When she asked to think it over the weekend and talk to her mother, he spent about 14 minutes arguing that seeking her mother's advice was the antithesis of what she needed to do before finally agreeing to a Monday follow-up; she did not enroll.
coverage: Full 1:03:47 transcript reviewed (352 segments, 100 percent read). One conversation, one prospect. Audio dropped from 14:11 to 20:43 (about 6.5 minutes unrecorded) and the prospect rejoined from her phone around 35:20-36:48. Speaker labels are scrambled in several places (e.g. Jack's 'not everyone gets the spot' and his monthly-income question are labelled as Ayshia); attribution above was corrected by context. No recording-consent statement was observed. No application or enrollment agreement was reached, so 14-day cancellation and agreement-reading checks were not applicable.

findings.quote: after finishing, a complete beginner usually lands their first role within three to six weeks. That first role is junior position. Juniors, they're starting around that like 70k a year role. And those roles are completely remote
findings.note: Presents a 3-6 week time-to-job, a ~$70K starting salary and fully remote roles as the expected outcome; these are P14 claims to remove.

findings.quote: From junior, our students typically get promoted to a senior position within six, nine months. And the seniors, those are the people who are going to be in that six figure range.
findings.note: Implies rapid progression to senior and six-figure pay within 6-9 months without evidence.

findings.quote: Let's say 12 months from now, you've done it, right? You're in a position where you have built that skill set. You're making six figures from that skill set
findings.note: Future-pacing exercise anchors the prospect on six figures within 12 months, an unsubstantiated salary expectation.

findings.quote: in this bootcamp, Ayshia, we actually place you in two paid internships with AI tech companies that we partner with. Yes, you're getting paid.
findings.note: Two paid internships are promised unconditionally with no mention of selection, eligibility, capacity or timing (P14: 'Everyone gets the internship').

findings.quote: you're going to build and sell projects for businesses anywhere from 500 bucks to 1500 bucks each... You're earning extra income from week two.
findings.note: Earn-while-you-learn income of $500-$1,500 per project from week two is presented as expected rather than possible.

findings.quote: they get a full refund of the tuition plus an additional $1,000 on top... You got to actually complete the bootcamp. You got to apply to a certain number of positions on a weekly basis.
findings.note: Job Guarantee described without the specific requirements (30 applications per week for 6 months, documented job search); the $65K floor and $1,000 bonus should be verified against the written guarantee.

findings.quote: you think that you're ready to take action? Like, we have a money back guarantee in place as well, if it doesn't work out.
findings.note: Uses the guarantee as a risk-free close after the prospect asked to think it over, without restating its conditions or how a refund interacts with the loan.

findings.quote: Once you land the job, you either keep making those small monthly payments or do what most students do is use a few paychecks to pay it off sooner.
findings.note: Tells the prospect most students pay the loan off with a few paychecks, a P14 claim to remove.

findings.quote: It's there to cover the monthlies until you land the job. The job covers the tuition.
findings.note: States the future job covers the tuition, implying the loan takes care of itself.

findings.quote: it'd be like a 60 month term, but people pay it off after month seven or eight once they get into the new job... So nobody ever pays it off for longer than like seven or eight months.
findings.note: Misrepresents the 60-month loan as effectively a 7-8 month obligation and asserts no one pays longer, which is unverifiable and understates the commitment.

findings.quote: all of our students use our funding partner. So you put no money down for the first time. A month and a half. And then after that, then the monthly payments are about 250 bucks.
findings.note: Monthly payment and deferral quoted without lender terms, interest or finance charge, and without saying the estimate may change after the application.

findings.quote: How that income is then meant to be used is you spend part of it on whatever you want, put the other part towards the monthly payments until you land the job.
findings.note: Presents earn-while-you-learn and internship income as the expected source of loan payments, tying repayment to uncertain program earnings.

findings.quote: No, no, it's like, like 30% or something.
findings.note: Claims only about 30% of applicants are offered a spot, an unsubstantiated selectivity claim used to make the offer feel scarce.

findings.quote: You're going to practice the technical questions that way you're going to walk in prepared. You're going to knock it out. You're going to land the role.
findings.note: Tells the prospect she is going to land the role, implying career support equals job placement.

findings.quote: as long as you can give me like five to 10 hours a week, I know that we can help you reach your goals... where you can actually earn the more money
findings.note: Frames success and higher income as assured given 5-10 hours a week, with no results-not-guaranteed qualifier.

findings.quote: going and asking them for like advice on it is almost like, like the anthesis... of what it is you need to do. Because they're going to say, stay at a risk.
findings.note: Discourages the prospect from seeking advice from her mother after she twice asked to think it over and consult a trusted person.

findings.quote: Do you think putting that decision or portion of it in somebody who hasn't even, doesn't even know what we're doing here, put a decision in them? Their hands is like what is the best idea
findings.note: Pushes back on the prospect's stated wish to consult someone she trusts, discouraging independent advice.

findings.quote: do you think that analyzing is going to get you to where you want to go, or do you think that action is going to get you to where you want to go?
findings.note: Frames the request for time to think as the obstacle to success, pressuring the prospect to decide on the call.

findings.quote: What do you think she'll say when you tell her that it's a 10k loan? ... And how is she going to know if it's a good fit?
findings.note: Pre-empts and undermines the parent's anticipated objection to the $10K loan instead of respecting the request to consult her.

findings.quote: Ayshia, how much longer do you want to keep missing out on your full potential?... you keep allowing this kind of like jumping around and I guess procrastination to hold you back and control you.
findings.note: Shaming language about procrastination used to build urgency before any program or price information.

findings.quote: you're not dumb. You know what I mean? Speaking candidly, like, you're You're not a silly person. Like, you know that this would help you out.
findings.note: Pressure framing that equates hesitation with being unintelligent, roughly 11 minutes after the prospect asked to think over the weekend.

findings.quote: They're across a few different time zones, so they'll always be there when you've got questions... You can book in as many calls as you want for one-to-one support.
findings.note: 'Always be there' and unlimited two-hour one-to-one bookings overstate support availability; should match actual hours and response times.

findings.quote: this program is three months long... If you put in 40 hours a week, you finish the setting off in four or five weeks.
findings.note: Program framed as a fixed three months while also self-paced; duration at 5-10 hours per week may differ materially from three months.

findings.quote: Don't get on board. You're going to get left behind.
findings.note: Absolute AI labour-market framing used to create urgency.

findings.quote: Well, the two main companies that we're partnered with, they're both like nine figure companies. One's called Skinstrick.
findings.note: Prospect assumed partnerships with Apple and Google; the closer pivoted to the real partners but never expressly corrected the assumption.

compliant.note: Asked directly whether she is sure she wants a software developer job before pitching, and probed her motivation at length.
Stated that the guarantee requires completing the bootcamp and applying to positions weekly, and that 'this isn't a magic pill... you still have to do the work'.
Said 'there's no crystal ball. You can't predict the future' when asking whether the program fits.
Described support as a team of 15 software engineers across time zones, not a single 24/7 mentor.
Clarified the internship is project-based, not full-time, and 'isn't going to be where the six figures come from'.
Stated the full $10K tuition, the ~$250 monthly payment and the 60-month term before any application or signature.
Said he did not want to give the impression earn-while-you-learn covers the full tuition: 'I've seen it happen, but usually it doesn't'.
Set the 5-10 hours per week commitment clearly and confirmed the prospect could meet it.
Named the actual partner company rather than affirming the prospect's Apple/Google assumption.
Repeated 'You don't have to' when the prospect said she should take the risk.
Ultimately agreed to let her think over the weekend and scheduled a Monday follow-up with no application started.
No SSN, date of birth, card number or address was read aloud; no lender application was opened on the call.

title: Zen × Jeff
summary: Jeff, a 51-year-old warehouse supervisor with existing student debt, enrolled on a Climb loan at about $262 a month. The call was not high-pressure, but the Job Guarantee was explained without any of its requirements, the closer told him what income figure to enter on the lender application, and both the lender disclosure and the loan agreement were accepted without being read.
coverage: Entire 332-line transcript reviewed. The recording ends mid-sentence at 47:57 during autopay setup, before the guarantee agreement was signed and the onboarding call was booked, so the close of the call cannot be verified. The prospect is hard of hearing and asked the closer to repeat himself at least eight times.

findings.quote: For whatever reason, you're not able to land a position at a minimum of 60K per year, what we will then do is give you a full refund of the tuition, plus $1,000. The only caveat, though, you have to actually do the work.
findings.note: The guarantee is presented with 'the only caveat' being effort. No mention of 30 applications a week, the six-month duration, documenting the search, completing the bootcamp, or the 12-month window.

findings.quote: Because you make over $60,000 a year, it doesn't change. So you can just put $60,000 for yearly income.
findings.note: Closer instructs the applicant what to enter as income on the Climb application and asserts how the lender underwrites. Jeff's actual income is roughly $70k to $75k.

findings.quote: Do you see how it says finance charge? Don't freak out about that. You can offset that because you're going to be able to pay this off in a faster way. I just have to tell you from a compliance perspective.
findings.note: The one moment the Truth in Lending disclosure was on screen, the student was told not to worry about it. APR and total finance charge were never read out.

findings.quote: Hit the box that says I agree. Leave electronically on. Hit submit.
findings.note: Student directed to tick 'I agree' on the lender disclosure and submit with no pause to read it.

findings.quote: Click agree? Yep.
findings.note: The loan agreement was accepted while the closer made small talk about camping. That exchange is the entire review of the agreement.

findings.quote: August, September, October. Well, we could be getting prepped, getting to the last month of education, getting ready for a job by November.
findings.note: On an October 9 call this implies job-ready in about seven weeks, which contradicts the three-month program described a minute later.

findings.quote: Three to six weeks after this period, we then see our complete beginners coming in and landing the first junior developer role, 60 to 80k per year, four to six hours per day, 100% remote. Six to eight months, senior position, around 150k.
findings.note: A full timeline with salaries attached, hedged only with 'on average' and 'if applied correctly'. Matches two phrases on the audit's remove-immediately list.

findings.quote: Based off the data, students start landing jobs between monthly payment three and monthly payment four.
findings.note: Links the job timeline to loan repayments, implying the loan is covered by employment income soon after it starts.

findings.quote: Full bootcamp and guaranteed job for 10K.
findings.note: The guarantee is a conditional refund, not a guaranteed job.

findings.quote: Hit set up autopay. This will serve two: one, where we send the money for the paid internships, and two, where in six weeks the monthly payment would come out of.
findings.note: The Climb autopay link is for loan repayment only. FES does not pay internship income through the lender's bank connection.

findings.quote: Time out, time out, Jeff. Can't be both, man. Excuse, excuse, excuse.
findings.note: Response to the student saying he still has bills to pay. Shuts down a financial concern instead of addressing it; he is adding a $10k loan on top of $50k in student debt.

findings.quote: You were kind of talking fast.
findings.note: Jeff said at 04:54 that he is hard of hearing and had misunderstood the hours commitment. He then completed a loan application on his phone to rapid click-by-click instructions. Weak informed-consent position.

findings.quote: You can have this life. It's not far away. It's a few months of grit.
findings.note: Aspirational framing that presents the outcome as near-certain.

findings.quote: $500 to around $1,000 a website.
findings.note: Earn-while-you-learn figure presented as expected. Other closers quote $250–$1,000 and $500–$1,500; no consistent, substantiated number.

findings.quote: An AI skincare company called Skinstrict.
findings.note: Internship partner named differently by each closer (Jax: 'AI tech companies', Karuna: 'SkinCentric'). Verify against what is documented.

Chat support, group coaching and unlimited bookable one-on-ones seven days a week. No 'one mentor 24/7' or 'daily call' claim.
Described modestly, no 'industry recognised' language.
Explicitly said this is not 'magically click some buttons and get rich'.

title: Karuna × Janet
summary: Karuna ran a discovery and pitch call with Janet, a 53-year-old optician working two jobs who said she is in financial distress; no enrollment or lender application happened and a follow-up was booked for Saturday. The call contains prohibited expected-outcome claims (job in 3-8 weeks, $60-90K remote starting salary, senior at $120-160K eight months later) and the 'pay off the loan with your first paychecks / three websites cover your payments' framing, though the guarantee requirements, tuition and monthly estimate were disclosed and no pressure was applied at the end.
coverage: Reviewed the full Fathom transcript (355 segments, 00:12 to 59:59, one conversation). Speaker labels are scrambled in places: several Karuna lines are attributed to Janet (e.g. 00:42, 53:25-54:00) and vice versa, so attribution was inferred from content. Audio is garbled around 52:46-53:25 (the 'guaranteed job of minimum six' line). No enrollment agreement or loan application was opened on this call, so the 14-day cancellation disclosure and agreement-reading rules were not applicable yet; they should be checked on the Saturday follow-up. No recording-consent statement appears in the transcript (a Zoom notice may have been shown but is not captured).

findings.quote: anywhere between three to eight weeks after the bootcamp to get the first job as a frontend developer. Now your starting salary is going to be between 60 to 90,000 a year, and that's a fully remote job.
findings.note: A specific time-to-job window, a starting salary band, a fully remote role and 4-6 hour workdays are presented as what the prospect should expect, with only a thin 'on average' hedge.

findings.quote: eight months later, you can start your promotion into a senior position if you'd like to. Typically that's going to take you to around 120 to 160 K per year.
findings.note: Implies rapid progression to a senior salary within months of a first job, without any substantiation that FES graduates achieve this.

findings.quote: three to five of these monthly payments before you get the job... you can take a portion of the first few paychecks from this job. You can use that to pay off the rest of the tuition.
findings.note: The loan is framed as something only 3-5 payments are made on before a job pays it off with the first paychecks, which is the prohibited 'loan pays itself' framing tied to an expected time-to-job.

findings.quote: if you want to build and sell maybe three websites, that will give you enough money to cover your monthly payments until you get this job. And then after you get it, you can pay off the rest.
findings.note: Earn-while-you-learn freelance income is presented as covering the loan payments, implying the financing takes care of itself regardless of the student's own means.

findings.quote: It will take you, you know, several months to get to 60K and then maybe like a year later, then get to like 100K as well.
findings.note: A salary and timeframe path (60K in months, 100K a year later) is stated as what will happen to this prospect rather than as a possible outcome.

findings.quote: if you are someone who comes in, does the work, know, finishes the program and does everything that's required, then yes, you know, there will be that guaranteed job.
findings.note: The conditional refund is described as a 'guaranteed job'; the actual refund terms were only explained later at 47:43, and FES does not control hiring.

findings.quote: let's say you get super unlucky and you don't get a job of minimum $60,000. Then you'll get a full refund of everything you pay plus $1,000. And we canceled the loan as well.
findings.note: States the loan is cancelled on refund without explaining how the refund interacts with the lender balance, interest or fees, which presents the financed program as effectively risk-free.

findings.quote: Oh, okay. No worries. Well, look, overall, I mean, you're still in a good position. What I recommend you do, what every student does, is a pre-approval on the full tuition.
findings.note: The prospect had said she is 'drowning', has no money, a falling credit score (~530) and cannot afford car payments, yet is told she is in a good position and steered straight to a full-tuition loan pre-approval.

findings.quote: You can. Obviously, it takes time and, you know, obviously effort to get there. But six figures is very achievable in this space, especially.
findings.note: Confirms a six-figure income as 'very achievable' for a complete beginner without any FES outcome data to back it.

findings.quote: We put every student into a paid internship... you can't get a job in this industry. With our experience, okay, it's impossible to do that.
findings.note: Says every student receives a paid internship and makes an absolute claim that getting hired without it is impossible; neither is stated with eligibility, selection or pay details.

findings.quote: you can sell websites anywhere between $250 to $1,000 per website. So it's very lucrative for our students. And it's a great way to make a little bit of extra income on the side as well.
findings.note: Earn-while-you-learn figures are presented as typical and 'very lucrative' without saying how many students actually earn this.

findings.quote: you'll get full access to your coach. So let's say you wanted a one-on-one Zoom call every single day. You probably don't need that. But if you want, you can, okay?
findings.note: Promises availability for a one-on-one call every day; students can book calls, but a daily one-on-one is not a committed service level. Mentors from TikTok, Google, Meta and Canva are also name-dropped in a way that implies affiliation.

findings.quote: your frontend simplified Institute of Technology certificate, which is a fully recognized certification in the space just to make your resume strong.
findings.note: Claims the FES certificate is a 'fully recognized certification', which is on the list of claims to remove unless industry recognition is documented.

findings.quote: she's making $65,000 in her very first remote job... So if you follow exactly what they've done, you'll get the same results. That's the most important thing, right?
findings.note: Individual graduate stories (Beth, 64, $65K remote; Chris, 42) are presented with an explicit promise that following the same steps yields the same results, implying these outcomes are typical.

findings.quote: your guaranteed job of minimum six [...] We keep working with you no matter how long it takes to get your six-figure job done.
findings.note: Describes the guarantee outcome as a 'six-figure job' when the agreement's threshold is a $60K offer; audio is partly garbled here so wording is uncertain.

findings.quote: no one pays this upfront because we work closely with different [finance] partners to make sure you get the cheapest approvals on your monthly payment. Now monthly payments are usually around $200, depending on your term.
findings.note: The ~$200 monthly figure is used as the anchor for the whole financing discussion, but the loan term, interest rate, finance charge and total repayment are never mentioned.

findings.quote: typically, we reply back within three to five minutes at any time of the day... schedule a Zoom call with your coach... it's available 24-7, and it's one-on-one as well.
findings.note: A 3-5 minute response time at any hour and 24-7 one-on-one call availability are stated as standard; these should match the actual delivered service level.

findings.quote: we're going to ask you to apply to 30 developer jobs every week using the outreach method that we have... you document your job search
findings.note: The 30-per-week requirement is explained but not its 6-month duration or the 12-month guarantee window, so the prospect does not hear the full eligibility conditions.

findings.quote: So I'll just say worst case, you need a $500. If you somehow get lucky, you might not need that.
findings.note: Down payment is framed as a matter of luck; the closer earlier correctly said it depends on the credit check, but the deposit rules should be stated as lender terms, not chance.

compliant.note: Walked through the refund agreement on screen: complete coursework, portfolio and resume approved before job search, 30 applications per week, documented search, refund of everything paid plus $1,000 if no $60K offer. Duration and 12-month window were missing (see low finding).
Stated the program price (around $10K) before any lender application or pressure.
Gave an estimated monthly payment range ($200-$250) before asking the prospect to apply, hedged with 'usually', 'typically' and 'depending on your term'.
Said that if the student does not put in the work nothing will happen and that it will not happen overnight.
Told the prospect FES does not want anyone to come in planning on the refund and that the refund is only a structure, not the goal.
Described the program as custom pace with 7-10 hours a week recommended and said progress depends on hours invested.
Described mentors as working a rotating 24-7 US shift pattern rather than one mentor available around the clock.
Live weekly coaching calls described as optional and recorded.
Said the down payment depends on credit and 'we'd have to check and see, to be honest' before giving a rough range.

compliant.area: No pressure to close on the call
compliant.note: Prospect was sick and asked to end the call; the closer did not push for an application or signature and scheduled a follow-up for Saturday evening.

compliant.area: Did not request SSN, DOB or card data
compliant.note: No Social Security number, date of birth, card number or loan application id was read aloud on the recording.
